## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Pādañjalījātaka* (Ja 247) is a narrative belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Pali Tipiṭaka [SuttaCentral]. According to the commentary, the Buddha related this story while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Elder Lāḷudāyī [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879a]. In the tale, Prince Pādañjali repeatedly twists his lip whenever decisions are delivered; the Bodhisatta, acting as a wise counselor, at first wonders whether the prince is profoundly wise and perceives subtle legal subtleties, uttering the first verse (*Addhā Pādañjali sabbe paññāya atirocati*) [Fausböll 1879a]. Upon testing him further, the ministers discover that the prince understands nothing at all apart from twisting his lip (*aññatra otthanibbhogā nāyaṁ jānāti kiñcanaṁ*), leading them to bypass the foolish prince and consecrate the Bodhisatta as king [Fausböll 1879a]. At the conclusion of the story, the Buddha identifies Pādañjali with Lāḷudāyī and the wise counselor with himself [Fausböll 1879a].
The opening verse and the Jātaka itself are cited elsewhere in the commentary on the Jātaka collection to exemplify a dull-witted person (*mandapañño bālo*) who is incapable of retaining royal honor or inherited family property [Fausböll 1891]. SuttaCentral lists four translations across four modern languages [SuttaCentral]. No Pali-internal text reuse matches or cross-language parallels in Chinese, Tibetan, or Sanskrit are listed by SuttaCentral or detected by DharmaNexus [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
